newsitem.title: GERMANY: Thousands of Bosnian refugees leave Germany.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of Bosnian refugees leave Germany.

text.p: Tens of thousands of refugees who fled the civil war in former Yugoslavia have returned home as a result of pressure from cash-strapped German states, according to official data released on Tuesday.
More than one-fifth of the 323,000 Bosnians who came to Germany during the 43-month war in the Balkans have gone back, officials from 16 state interior ministries said.

Despite widespread international criticism, the states began forcibly repatriating refugees late last year after efforts to encourage voluntary returns failed. The pressure to leave or face deportation apparently prompted many to go on their own.

A Reuters survey of state governments found that about 65,000 refugees have since left Germany and about 408 have been forcibly deported. About half of those sent against their will had been convicted of crimes in Germany.

"We didn't expect to have such a big number until the fall," said Christoph Hillebrand, spokesman for the Bavarian interior ministry. "And the actual number is probably quite a bit higher than the number we have recorded."

Bavaria, which has been particularly aggressive in forcing the refugees to leave, said that 21,000 have returned from the southern state to their home country since November. Bavaria has also deported 172 people.
Germany, haunted by its own painful memories of war and its aftermath, took in about 323,000 people during the 1992-95 Bosnian war -- more than the rest of the European Union put together.

Most Germans welcomed the refugees with enthusiasm, providing shelter and about 1,000 marks ($537) per family per month in spending money, cash that many stashed away and sent to relatives who stayed behind in Bosnia.
But after the fighting stopped in 1995, the welcoming arms began to grow weary. German states paying to support the refugees were disappointed only a handful returned home.

After the Dayton peace accord was signed in late 1995 the states said they could no longer afford the estimated four billion marks it costs each year to support the refugees. The 30,000 refugees in Berlin cost the near-bankrupt state 500 million marks per year.

Most refugees elected to remain in Germany because of fears fighting would break out again in the Balkans or their homes had been destroyed. Others feared poverty or said their home towns were now controlled by other ethnic groups.

Frustrated by the refugees' reluctance to return home, the states last October said they would start deporting those who did not return voluntarily, although many of the 16 states waited until the winter had passed.
To encourage the Bosnians to return home, many states offer cash premiums that can exceed several hundred marks per person to cover their transport and resettlement costs.

"Many families have taken advantage of our offer to send an advance member of the family home first to examine the area they are planning to go to," said Ludger Harmeier, spokesman for the North Rhine-Westphalia state interior ministry.
About 14,300 of the 72,600 Bosnian refugees who spent the war in Germany's most populous state have since returned home, Harmeier said.
Seven smaller states, which have relatively few refugees, have not deported any refugees, authorities said.
